q: Two tanks of identical juice are pitched with different commercial strains and smell nothing alike a fortnight later. What is the strain actually doing to produce that?
opts: Freeing odourless precursors, and adding by-products of its own
Turning the aroma of one variety into that of another grape
Drawing aroma compounds out of the walls of the steel tank
Contributing varietal aromas bred in, which the juice lacked
exp: A great deal of a wine's aroma arrives bound to sugars or amino acids and has no smell at all until a yeast enzyme cuts it loose, and strains differ sharply in how much they release. On top of that the yeast make esters and higher alcohols of their own, which is why strain choice is a genuine stylistic decision.

q: Bottled in a hurry, a red that had not finished its bacterial conversion reaches the shelf faintly hazy and prickling on the tongue. What has gone on inside the bottle?
opts: Tartrates came out of solution in a cold warehouse and clouded the wine
The yeast found sugar they had missed and ran a second alcoholic ferment in the bottle
Air drawn in past the cork oxidised the wine and dropped a brown deposit with it
The conversion carried on there, throwing carbon dioxide and a bacterial haze
exp: Bacteria left alive in a wine that still holds malic acid will finish the job wherever they happen to be, and in a sealed bottle the carbon dioxide they throw off has nowhere to go. A cellar therefore either sees the conversion right through in tank, confirming it by chromatography or an enzymatic test rather than by taste, or filters the bacteria out before the wine goes anywhere near the filler.

q: A cellar wants the bacterial conversion finished before winter cold shuts it down. Which pair of conditions encourages it?
opts: A cold cellar and no sulphur dioxide at all
A warm cellar and a high level of sulphur dioxide
A cold cellar and a high level of sulphur dioxide
A warm cellar and a low level of sulphur dioxide
exp: The bacteria work best at around eighteen to twenty-two degrees, slow almost to a stop below fifteen and are held back by free sulphur dioxide, so a cellar creates or removes those two conditions depending on what it wants. Preventing the conversion in a wine meant to stay sharp is exactly the same knowledge applied in reverse.

q: Immediately after fermentation a vessel holds a coarse sediment of skin fragments, pulp and dead yeast, and a much finer one settles later. Why is the coarse fraction usually taken away early?
opts: It would restart the fermentation once the wine is moved
It can strip oxygen from the wine and throw sulphurous smells
It holds the wine's colour, which returns during ageing
It makes the finished wine taste sweet and flat
exp: Gross lees are dense and biologically active, and a wine left sitting on them can develop off-smells within weeks. The first racking is therefore timed in days rather than months, and a cellar judges the moment by smelling the tank rather than by the calendar, since a warm vessel turns faster than a cold one.

q: Two identical barrels are filled from one tank; one is left sitting on its fine sediment and the other is drawn off clean. Which stays fresher for longer with no extra sulphur, and why?
opts: The clean one, because the sediment draws oxygen into the barrel
The clean one, because the sediment raises the wine's pH over time
The one on its sediment, because the yeast cells take up oxygen
Neither, because the sediment has no bearing on how the wine oxidises
exp: Lees act as a natural antioxidant, which is part of why wines raised on them can be handled with a lighter hand on added sulphur. That protection vanishes the moment the wine is moved away from them, so the racking date is also a sulphur decision.

q: Every fortnight through the winter one barrel of white has its sediment roused back into suspension with a rod while its neighbour is left undisturbed. What should separate them at the table?
opts: The roused barrel ends up deeper in colour
The roused barrel tastes rounder and creamier in texture
The undisturbed barrel finishes higher in alcohol
The roused barrel tastes distinctly sweeter than its neighbour
exp: Putting the sediment back into suspension multiplies the wine's contact with it, and the compounds released build weight across the middle of the palate. It is a lever with a price, since a heavily worked barrel trades some of its aromatic lift for that texture, and fashion has swung back towards restraint.

q: Unlined concrete tanks shaped like eggs have replaced steel in some cellars for whites raised without oak. Beyond the thermal steadiness of a thick wall, what is the shape meant to do?
opts: Increase the surface of wine in contact with the air
Allow the grapes to be pressed inside the vessel itself
Compress the wine at the base so that it falls bright faster
Set up a slow convection current that keeps the fine sediment moving
exp: With no corners to trap anything, the tank is said to circulate gently on its own and give something of the effect of stirring with nobody touching it. Concrete's uncontested virtue is mass, since a heavy wall holds temperature steady through a warm cellar and contributes no flavour whatever.

q: Wine raised in unglazed earthenware behaves unlike the same wine in a steel tank of equal size. What is the clay contributing?
opts: A slow exchange of oxygen through the porous wall
Vanilla and toast, drawn out of the fired clay itself
A measurable rise in the wine's acidity over the months
A faster and warmer fermentation than steel
exp: Porosity puts a clay vessel between a barrel and a tank: the wine breathes, but nothing is seasoned into it. Producers who want the neutrality without the air line or wax the interior precisely to shut that exchange down.

q: An inexpensive red shows clear vanilla and toast, yet the producer owns no barrels at all. How was that done?
opts: A longer fermentation on the skins
Ageing in unlined concrete tanks
A dose of oenological tannin
Oak chips or staves left in the tank
exp: Chips, staves and inserts deliver oak flavour cheaply and quickly, and at the bottom of the market they are the rule rather than the exception. What they cannot give is the slow maturation a barrel provides alongside its flavour, so the oak arrives on a wine that has not been changed in any other way. Toast level and oak origin are specified much as they would be for a barrel, and the dose is set in grams per litre.

q: Cooling jackets wrap the outside of a stainless tank and chilled glycol runs through them. Which ability does steel hand the winemaker that a wooden vat cannot?
opts: A slow trickle of oxygen through the vessel wall
A lower final acidity in the finished wine
Fast, precise control of fermentation temperature
Flavour compounds drawn from the vessel itself
exp: Steel conducts heat quickly, so a ferment can be held within a degree of a target and a tank can be chilled hard whenever the cellar chooses. Wood insulates instead, which is why coolers have to be dropped inside a wooden vat rather than strapped around it.

q: Open wooden vats still stand in cellars that could afford any equipment they liked. What do they offer that a closed steel tank does not for a red ferment?
opts: They keep the wine entirely free of oxygen during the ferment
They make chilling the ferment easier than steel
They let fermentation begin without any yeast at all
They hold their warmth and let the cap be worked by hand
exp: An open top is what makes plunging possible at all, and thick staves keep a ferment warm overnight without any heating. The cost is that everything above the wine line is exposed to the air, so the cap can never be left to itself.

q: A ceramic diffuser feeds a fine, metered stream of oxygen into a tank of young red over several months. What is that treatment set up to achieve?
opts: Tannin softened and colour fixed in months, not years
An increase in the wine's alcohol, since oxygen feeds the yeast
The removal of the wine's carbon dioxide, left over from the ferment
A second fermentation, since the oxygen wakes the sleeping yeast
exp: Micro-oxygenation imitates the trickle of air a barrel supplies, at a rate the cellar sets in milligrams per litre per month. Overdone it dries the wine out and ages it before its time, so the dose is tiny and the tank is tasted constantly.

q: Pressed white juice is deliberately splashed and aerated until it browns in the tank, before any yeast goes anywhere near it. Why is that not the disaster it looks?
opts: Browning raises the acidity of the juice
The yeast consume the oxygen later in the ferment, and the brown colour is reversed as the wine falls bright
The compounds that brown drop out before fermentation, so the finished wine holds its colour better
The brown pigment settles into the sediment and is stirred back in
exp: Hyperoxidation sacrifices the phenolics that would otherwise have oxidised in bottle: they polymerise and settle out with the juice solids, and whatever brown survives is taken down onto the yeast and lees during fermentation rather than being reversed, so the wine ships more stable than juice protected all the way through. It costs some aromatic detail, which is why it suits neutral varieties and not perfumed ones.

q: Before wine is moved into an empty vessel, the tank is flushed with an unreactive gas and the headspace kept full of it afterwards. What is being protected?
opts: The wine's temperature, by insulating it from the cellar
The wine's clarity, by settling the particles faster
The wine's sparkle, by holding it under gas pressure
The wine's fruit aroma and colour, by keeping oxygen off it
exp: Carbon dioxide, nitrogen and argon are all used for this, and a cellar working reductively will flush hoses, presses and bottling lines as well as tanks. Whites and roses gain the most from it, since they have no tannin to spend defending themselves.

q: An actively fermenting vat is remarkably safe from oxidation even with the lid off and nothing added to it. What is defending the wine?
opts: The blanket of carbon dioxide the yeast throw off
The alcohol, which is too stable a molecule to oxidise
The heat of the ferment, which drives the oxygen out
The sugar still in solution, which soaks up air
exp: Fermentation throws off a heavy blanket of gas that sits on the wine and pushes air out of the vessel, which is also why an enclosed fermentation cellar is genuinely dangerous to walk into. The protection ends the moment fermentation does, and that is when a winemaker's attention to oxygen properly begins.

q: A tank is pumped deliberately through the air into another vessel, splashing as it falls, rather than being moved gently across. What is the cellar after?
opts: A rise in the wine's temperature as it falls through the air
A dose of oxygen, to drive off sulphur compounds and open the wine up
A finer sediment in the receiving tank, since the wine falls hard
A faster transfer, since wine falling through air moves quicker
exp: Splash racking treats oxygen as a tool rather than a threat, and a wine closed up from too little air will often clean up within hours of it. The same handling given to a delicate white with nothing to hide simply tires it out.
